P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: No. Singapore has no exchange controls. There are no limits on repatriation, remittances or foreign-exchange transactions, and no surrender or conversion requirement for foreign receipts. MAS keeps some restrictions on non-residents' use of the Singapore dollar.

sources.quote: Exchange Arrangements and Controls Singapore applies no currency exchange controls, although the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) does enforce some restrictions on the use of non-domestic transactions for SGD.

P2_fcy_account.question: Can resident individuals hold a foreign-currency account locally?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Yes. Residents may hold foreign-currency accounts both in Singapore and abroad, and may also hold Singapore-dollar accounts abroad.

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: Sole proprietorships register with ACRA through BizFile+. Owners must be Singapore citizens, permanent residents or eligible FIN holders. Foreigners living overseas must use a corporate service provider and appoint a locally resident authorised representative. Registration costs $100 for one year or $160 for three years; the three-year option depends on CPF conditions. Renewal costs $30 a year. Self-employed owners must keep MediSave contributions up to date or ACRA cannot renew and may cancel the registration.

L2_tax_id.question: Tax ID: who needs one, how to get it?
L2_tax_id.answer: No separate TIN is issued. Individuals are identified for tax by their NRIC (citizens and PRs) or FIN (foreigners). Registered businesses, including sole proprietorships, use the UEN issued at ACRA registration.

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Singapore taxes on a territorial, remittance basis. Since 1 January 2004, foreign-sourced income received in Singapore by resident individuals has been exempt, unless it comes through a Singapore partnership. Income from a business carried on in Singapore is Singapore-source even when the clients are abroad, so the exemption does not cover it. Resident rates are progressive from 0% on the first $20,000 to a top rate of 24% (from YA 2024).

sources.title: Taxation liability for Singaporeans with businesses and investments in other countries
sources.quote: Singapore adopts a territorial, remittance-based income tax system.

sources.title: Tax Exemption for Foreign-Sourced Income (e-Tax Guide)
sources.quote: 2.2 From 1 Jan 2004, all foreign- sourced income received in Singapore by resident individuals, except those received through a Singapore partnership, will be exempt from tax where the Comptroller is satisfied that the exemption will be beneficial to them.

sources.title: Individual income tax rates
sources.quote: The current highest personal income tax rate is at 24%.

L3_income_tax_foreign.notes: TRAP: a freelancer living and working in Singapore is generally carrying on a business in Singapore, so the income is not 'foreign-sourced' just because clients pay from abroad (inference from the territorial rule; no IRAS page on this captured).

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: GST is 9%. Registration is compulsory when taxable turnover exceeds S$1 million in a calendar year (retrospective view) or is expected to exceed it in the next 12 months (prospective view). Services count as international services, zero-rated at 0%, only if they fall within section 21(3) of the GST Act; many services contracted with and directly benefiting an overseas person qualify. A business whose taxable turnover is wholly or mainly zero-rated can apply for exemption from registration.

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law applicable to a small online business
L5_data_protection.answer: The Personal Data Protection Act 2012 applies, enforced by the PDPC. Organisations have no registration requirement, but must appoint a data protection officer and make their data-protection policies available. Since 1 October 2022, penalties can reach S$1 million, or 10% of Singapore turnover for organisations with turnover above S$10 million, whichever is higher.

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: Consumer-protection / e-commerce rules for online sales (refunds, disclosures)
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: The Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act covers online sellers and prohibits unfair practices; CCCS enforces it. There is no general statutory cooling-off period for ordinary online purchases, so change-of-mind returns depend on the seller's own policy. The 5-working-day cancellation right applies to direct sales and timeshare contracts.
L6_consumer_ecommerce.note: No-cooling-off statement from a single secondary domain (RecordingLaw); the official CCCS advisory only tells consumers to check each retailer's return/refund policy. CASE pages returned 403 on 2026-10-22.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: none of the major platform barriers apply. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Physical or digital goods on Etsy (Etsy seller payments are available here). (6) Client payments by PayPal (on PayPal's Payouts list as 'Fully localized'). (7) Stripe accepts merchants here, so you can take card payments directly on your own site. (8) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
